summaries.example: Imagine a balance scale with equal bags on both sides. If the scale stays level, you might ask why. Perhaps the bags weigh the same and are placed equally far from the middle. The Principle of Sufficient Reason says that there should be some explanation for what happens, rather than the balance staying level for no reason at all.
summaries.summary: The Principle of Sufficient Reason, often called the PSR, is the philosophical idea that every fact or event has a reason, cause, or explanation. For example, if one shop charges much more for the same item than another shop, we naturally ask why. Some versions of the PSR say that everything needs an explanation. Other versions cover only certain things, such as events, objects, or facts about whether something exists. Philosophers also disagree about what counts as a reason. It might be a cause, the nature of a thing, or a rule that makes something understandable. Spinoza used the principle to argue that existence and nonexistence need explanations. Leibniz gave the principle its familiar name and used it in arguments about God, space, time, and why the world is the way it is. The PSR is powerful, but it creates puzzles: Can anything explain itself? Can reasons continue forever? Or must some explanations end with basic facts?
key_ideas: The principle says that things should not simply happen for no reason.
Philosophers disagree about whether everything needs an explanation or only some things.
A reason might be a cause, a thing’s nature, or a deeper explanation.
Spinoza and Leibniz made this principle central to their philosophies.
The principle can lead to difficult questions about endless chains of reasons and things that explain themselves.
summaries.why_it_matters: The PSR helps us understand why people keep asking “Why?” in science and philosophy. It encourages careful investigation instead of giving up too quickly. But it also reminds us that a strong rule can create hard questions. If everything needs a reason, the rule itself may need a reason, and we must think about whether some facts could be basic or unexplained.

important_terms.definition: The idea that every fact, event, or thing has some reason, cause, or explanation.
Something that cannot be explained, even though it is true or happens.
An answer to the question “Why did this happen?” or “Why is this thing this way?”
A reason that is enough to account for something.

questions_to_think_about: Does every surprising event need an explanation?
Could there be a fact that has no reason at all?
If every reason needs another reason, where would the chain stop?
Is asking for reasons always helpful?
What should we do when we do not yet know an explanation?

summaries.example: Suppose two otherwise indistinguishable locations exist in an absolute space, and a creator places the universe at one rather than the other. Leibniz argues that there would be no sufficient reason for choosing one location instead of the other. Since a choice without a reason is unacceptable under the PSR, he uses this kind of case to support the view that space is relational rather than an independently existing container.
summaries.summary: The Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR) says, in its broadest form, that for every fact there is a sufficient reason why it obtains. The entry stresses that this is a family of principles rather than a single formula. A version may range over entities, propositions, events, or possibilities, and the relevant relation may be causal, epistemic, or metaphysical grounding. The principle may also be factive—claiming that reasons really exist—or regulative—requiring inquiry to proceed as though intelligible explanations should be sought. Spinoza and Leibniz are its central early-modern advocates. Spinoza treats existence and nonexistence as requiring explanation and allows infinite causal series, provided the entire contingent series is grounded in a necessarily existing being. Leibniz gives the principle its name and develops logical and metaphysical accounts of sufficient reason, including conceptual containment, primitive active force, and the Principle of the Best. He applies it to arguments for God, the Identity of Indiscernibles, and relational space and time. The PSR faces the Agrippan Trilemma: explanation seems to end in brute facts, continue without limit, or become self-explanation. Later philosophers restrict, criticize, or reformulate the principle, while contemporary discussions often express it through grounding.
key_ideas: The PSR is not one single doctrine: its scope may cover facts, propositions, entities, events, actual things, or even possibilities.
Versions differ in modal force. A strong version says the principle holds necessarily; a weaker version says it is only actually true.
A factive PSR asserts that explanations really exist, while a regulative PSR treats the demand for explanation as a rule for inquiry.
Spinoza emphasizes explanations of both existence and nonexistence and permits infinite causal chains if the whole chain is grounded in what exists necessarily.
Leibniz connects the PSR with his theories of truth, contingency, active force, and the best possible world, though the relation among these accounts is debated.

The principle has been used to argue for claims such as God’s existence, the relational character of space and time, and the Identity of Indiscernibles; critics challenge whether these arguments succeed.
summaries.why_it_matters: The PSR concerns a basic standard of rational inquiry: whether reality is intelligible and whether unexplained facts are acceptable. It clarifies why philosophical arguments often move from a puzzling fact to a proposed ground, but it also exposes the risk of assuming what one is trying to prove. Its history shows how one principle can support very different metaphysical systems, from Spinoza’s necessitarianism to Leibniz’s account of contingency, and why the limits of explanation remain contested.

important_terms.definition: A broad philosophical principle stating that every fact, truth, event, or entity has a sufficient reason, cause, or ground.
A fact that has no explanation or reason, at least in the relevant sense.
An explanation in terms of what makes something the case, rather than merely what causes it in time.
True in all possible circumstances; its denial involves contradiction or conceptual impossibility.
True in some circumstances but not unavoidable; it could have been otherwise.
The view that there is only one genuinely possible way reality could be, often associated in the entry with Spinoza.
The claim that no two distinct things can have exactly the same properties or features.
The problem that explanation seems to require either unexplained starting points, an endless regress, or something that explains itself.

questions_to_think_about: Should the PSR apply to every truth, or only to events and contingent facts?
Does an infinite chain of explanations satisfy the PSR, or does the whole chain still need a further explanation?
Can a thing’s essence genuinely explain its existence, or does that merely restate the claim?
Does Leibniz’s argument against absolute space depend on the PSR, or on additional assumptions about divine choice?
Is a regulative demand to keep searching for explanations defensible even if some facts are ultimately brute?

summaries.example: You notice that your school’s alarm rings at 8:00 on some days but at 8:15 on others. You would probably ask what explains the difference: perhaps the schedule changes on certain days, or a special event is happening. A supporter of the PSR says this habit of looking for a reason should apply not only to alarms but, in some versions, to every fact. A critic may say that some facts might simply have no further explanation.
summaries.summary: The Principle of Sufficient Reason, or PSR, is the idea that things do not occur or exist without a reason. In its widest form, it says that every fact has a sufficient explanation. However, philosophers disagree about what the principle covers. It might apply to events, objects, true statements, existence, nonexistence, or even possible things. They also disagree about what a reason is: it could be a cause, a logical connection, or a deeper relation of dependence called grounding. Spinoza and Leibniz are especially important figures in the history of the PSR. Spinoza argues that a thing’s existence and nonexistence must be explainable, while allowing an infinite sequence of causes when the whole sequence has an ultimate ground. Leibniz names the principle and uses it to argue against unexplained choices, perfectly indistinguishable objects, and absolute space and time. The PSR is attractive because asking for reasons is part of ordinary thinking. It is controversial because applying it everywhere may lead to difficult choices between unexplained facts, infinite explanation, and self-explanation.
key_ideas: The PSR comes in several versions. Some cover everything, while others cover only certain facts, events, or objects.
Spinoza and Leibniz both gave the principle an important place, but interpreters disagree about exactly how Spinoza used it.
Spinoza held that both existence and nonexistence can require explanation and accepted some infinite chains of causes.
Leibniz used the PSR to argue that reality is not random and to support claims about God, space, time, and distinct objects.
A major challenge asks whether explanations must end in a basic fact, continue forever, or eventually explain themselves.
Some philosophers treat the PSR as a fact about reality; others treat it as a rule that guides investigation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The PSR helps explain why people do not usually accept “it just happened” as a complete answer. It supports the search for causes and deeper connections in science and philosophy. At the same time, it teaches us to examine our assumptions: demanding a reason for everything may produce bold conclusions, but it may also go beyond what our evidence can establish.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical rule saying that every fact or event has a reason, cause, or explanation.
A fact accepted as true even though no explanation for it is available or required.
The thing that needs explaining, such as an event, fact, object, or true statement.
The reason, cause, or fact that explains something else.
A statement that could have been different; it is not true in every possible situation.
A statement that could not be false without contradiction.
An explanation showing what something depends on or what makes it the case, not just what happened before it.

questions_to_think_about: Would finding no explanation for something prove that it has none?
Why might someone think that nonexistence needs an explanation as well as existence?
Can an endless series of reasons explain anything, or does the whole series need a reason?
Why does Leibniz think two perfectly alike things would create a problem for explanation?
Is it reasonable to use the PSR in science without claiming that we can know every reason?
